newsitem.title: ITALY: FOCUS - Italian economy slows, CPI scores own goal.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Italian economy slows, CPI scores own goal.

text.p: The sluggish Italian economy slowed in the second quarter of 1996 and showed continued signs of stagnation in the third quarter, but is not in recession, national statistics office Istat said on Friday.

Istat also said that the steady fall in the rate of inflation since the start of the year paused in September in the face of an unexpected jump in the price of tickets for premier division soccer matches.
Italy's gross domestic product (GDP) fell 0.4 percent between April and June compared with the first quarter. On a year-by-year basis the economy grew 0.7 percent.
The figures were slightly better than provisional data released in August had indicated, but still pointed to a struggling economy that was not about to improve, Istat said.

"From indicators available, consumer demand shows signs of being in a depressed state. In the third quarter, GDP is basically stationary," Enrico Giovannini, head of Istat's GDP statistics office, told reporters.
"We are in a phase of stagnation not recession," he added.
Faltering industrial output, strong lira gains since the start of the year and stringent Bank of Italy monetary policy have all combined to stall economic growth.

The government is hoping for a pick-up in the final three months of the year, but economists warn that the austerity budget presented to parliament by Treasury Minister Carlo Azeglio Ciampi on Thursday could unleash a full-blown recession.
The 1997 budget is designed to slash 62.5 trillion lire ($41 billion) off next year's deficit and includes a one-off "Euro tax", which is hoped will raise 13 trillion lire.
"On the growth side, a package of this size will have dire consequences," said Sally Wilkinson, a London-based economist at Swiss bank UBS.

Facing a fresh bout of fiscal severity, union and business leaders have urged Bank of Italy governor Antonio Fazio to cut the official discount rate and make the cost of borrowing money cheaper. However Fazio has indicated that inflation will have to fall beneath three percent for further monetary relaxation.

Lingering hopes that the consumer price index had edged towards the three percent level last month were dashed on Friday when Istat announced year-on-year inflation did not move from August's 3.4 percent.
The largest single rise was seen in the recreation sector, where prices rose 1.1 percent month-on-month after soccer clubs hiked their ticket prices at the start of the new season.
Despite the pause in the year-long decline in Italian inflation, analysts said the downward trend would continue and bring with it the much sought-after rate cut.

"We could see three percent as early as November but definitely in December, so we remain rather confident we will see a rate cut by year end," Lorenzo Codogno, head of research at Bank of America in Milan, told Reuters Financial Television.
"After the significant recent belt tightening I would expect a one percent cut," he added.
Italy's discount rate was last reduced in July, when Fazio lowered it to 8.25 percent from a previous nine percent. $=1,519 lire
